difficultyReason: Single-premise argument with one clear gap. The claim that increased advertising caused sales growth assumes no other factor (seasonal demand, competitor exit, price change) explains the sales increase.
stimulus: Economist: Our company increased its advertising spending by 40% last quarter, and sales revenue rose by 35% during that same period. Therefore, the increased advertising directly caused the rise in sales.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the economist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No other factor besides increased advertising contributed to the rise in sales revenue.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The company's competitors did not increase their advertising spending during the same period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The advertisements reached a large percentage of the target market.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sales revenue had been declining in previous quarters.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The 35% rise in sales was larger than anticipated.

explanations.correct: The argument infers causation from a temporal correlation: ad spending increased, then sales increased. For this inference to hold, the economist must assume that no other factor—seasonal uptick, price reduction, competitor failure, new product feature—explains the sales rise. Negate A: if other factors did contribute, the argument collapses.
explanations.B: Competitor behavior is irrelevant; the argument cares only whether ad spending caused *this* company's sales rise, not whether competitors also advertised.
explanations.C: The percentage of the target market reached is not invoked as evidence in the argument.
explanations.D: Previous quarters' performance is not required; the argument works whether sales were declining, stable, or rising before.
explanations.E: Whether the rise met expectations is irrelevant to the causal claim.

difficultyReason: Straightforward single-premise inference. A doctor concludes a patient's symptoms are psychosomatic; the gap is that medical tests ruled out physical causes, which the argument must assume to make the conclusion valid.
stimulus: Physician: Patient M has complained of chronic fatigue and body aches for two months. I have conducted a thorough physical examination and found no signs of infection, inflammation, or organ dysfunction. Therefore, the patient's symptoms are likely psychosomatic in origin.
questionStem: The physician's argument requires the assumption that

choices.label: A
choices.text: Psychosomatic symptoms are more common than physically caused symptoms.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The patient is not consciously fabricating symptoms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A thorough physical examination can rule out all major physical causes of fatigue and body aches.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Patients who are skeptical of psychiatric treatment are likely to have psychosomatic symptoms.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The patient's symptoms will resolve without pharmaceutical intervention.

explanations.correct: The physician's reasoning is: no physical causes found → symptoms are psychosomatic. This inference depends on the assumption that a thorough exam can actually rule out physical causes. Without C, there could be undetected physical conditions (rare diseases, subclinical infection, etc.), and the conclusion would be unsupported. Negate C: if the exam missed physical causes, the inference fails.
explanations.A: The prevalence of psychosomatic versus physical symptoms is irrelevant to diagnosing this patient.
explanations.B: Conscious fabrication (malingering) and psychosomatic symptoms are different; the argument doesn't invoke malingering.
explanations.D: Patient attitudes toward psychiatry are not mentioned or required.
explanations.E: Prognosis without drugs is not necessary for the diagnosis.

difficultyReason: Single-sentence argument with an obvious gap. Historian infers a manuscript's date from its subject matter; assumes that the subject (medieval warfare tactics) was not written about before or after the claimed period.
stimulus: Historian: This manuscript describes medieval warfare tactics and strategies in great detail. Medieval warfare was most prevalent in Europe between the 10th and 15th centuries. Therefore, this manuscript was likely written during the medieval period.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No one has written about medieval warfare tactics since the medieval period ended.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The manuscript's author was a European military officer.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Medieval warfare was more prevalent in Europe than in other parts of the world.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The physical condition of the manuscript indicates its age.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Medieval warfare tactics are not used in modern military practice.

explanations.correct: The argument infers date from subject matter: medieval-warfare content → medieval-period origin. This assumes that detailed descriptions of medieval tactics were not written outside the medieval period. If modern scholars wrote such detailed descriptions (A negated), the content alone cannot date the manuscript to the medieval period. Negate A and the argument fails.
explanations.B: The author's identity and profession are not invoked in the argument.
explanations.C: Geographic prevalence is mentioned but not required for the dating inference.
explanations.D: Physical condition is explicitly not mentioned as evidence.
explanations.E: Modern military use of medieval tactics is not discussed and not necessary for the argument.

difficultyReason: Simple conditional argument. If students don't study, they fail; student failed → student didn't study. The gap is that failure has no other cause.
stimulus: Teacher: Students who do not study for the final exam will fail the exam. Student X failed the exam. Therefore, Student X did not study for the exam.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most students who fail the final exam do not study.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Studying is the only factor that determines exam performance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The only reason a student would fail the exam is failure to study.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Student X had the opportunity to study before the exam.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The final exam is more difficult than previous exams.

explanations.correct: The argument reasons: not studying → failure. Then, failure → not studying (illicit reverse). This backward step requires assuming no other cause of failure exists. If a student could fail due to illness, test anxiety, or learning disability even while studying (C negated), the failure doesn't prove non-study. Negate C and the inference breaks.
explanations.A: Statistical frequency is irrelevant to whether this specific student studied.
explanations.B: Too strong — the argument only needs studying to be *a* cause, not *the only* determinant.
explanations.D: Opportunity is not mentioned and not required for the logical form.
explanations.E: Difficulty level is not invoked in the argument.

difficultyReason: Straightforward inference from a single observation. Lawyer concludes a law is effective because crime decreased after enactment; assumes the crime decrease was caused by the law, not by other factors.
stimulus: Legal analyst: The new anti-fraud law was enacted three years ago, and since then, reported instances of fraud in the financial sector have declined by 50%. Therefore, the new law has been highly effective in reducing fraud.
questionStem: The analyst's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The decline in reported fraud was primarily caused by the new law rather than by other factors.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fraud prevention was the primary goal of the legislature in enacting the law.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The financial sector did not experience unusually high fraud rates before the law was enacted.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All fraud in the financial sector is now reported to authorities.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The law will continue to be effective in reducing fraud in the future.

explanations.correct: The argument observes temporal correlation (law enacted → fraud declined) and infers causation (law caused decline). This requires assuming the law, not other causes (improved auditing technology, market downturn reducing fraud opportunities, increased enforcement resources), drove the decline. Negate A: if other factors caused the decline, the law's effectiveness is unsupported.
explanations.B: Legislative intent is not relevant to whether the law actually reduced fraud.
explanations.C: Baseline fraud rates before the law do not determine whether the law was effective after enactment.
explanations.D: Reporting completeness affects measurement but is not necessary for the causal inference.
explanations.E: Future effectiveness is not required for claiming present effectiveness.

difficultyReason: Simple environmental argument. Wildlife biologist observes a species thriving and concludes its habitat is healthy; assumes habitat health is the cause of thriving population, not vice versa or independent variables.
stimulus: Wildlife biologist: The river ecosystem is home to a diverse population of native fish species that have increased in number over the past five years. This growth demonstrates that the river's ecosystem is healthy.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A healthy river ecosystem can only support native fish species.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The increase in fish population did not cause the ecosystem's health but rather resulted from it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fish populations are more reliable indicators of ecosystem health than water quality measurements.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The river did not experience any harmful pollution events in the past five years.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Diverse populations of native fish require unpolluted water to survive.

explanations.correct: The argument reasons: thriving fish population → healthy ecosystem. This assumes health is the cause of thriving populations, not the reverse (a thriving population creating its own conditions) or mutual dependence. If population increase somehow caused ecosystem health rather than vice versa (B negated), the inference would be backwards. Negate B and the causal direction collapses.
explanations.A: The argument doesn't claim exclusive relationship; other organisms can coexist.
explanations.C: The argument doesn't compare fish to other indicators; it uses fish as evidence.
explanations.D: Absence of pollution is a separate claim; the argument relies on the causal link between health and population, not pollution history.
explanations.E: Too strong — the argument only needs a plausible connection, not an absolute requirement.

difficultyReason: One-premise argument about linguistic change. Speaker concludes a language evolves because it has been spoken for centuries; assumes stability or slow change is not the default outcome of long language use.
stimulus: Linguist: English has been spoken continuously for over a thousand years and has evolved significantly in vocabulary, pronunciation, and grammar. Therefore, languages naturally evolve over time.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: English is representative of all spoken languages.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A language spoken for a thousand years is more likely to evolve than one spoken for a shorter period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Languages do not remain static over long periods of continuous use.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Evolution in pronunciation is a more significant change than evolution in vocabulary.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The speakers of English have always valued linguistic innovation.

explanations.correct: The argument observes that English evolved over a millennium and concludes languages naturally evolve. This assumes that evolution is not merely coincidental but that languages inherently change with time. Negate C: if languages can remain static over centuries, then English's evolution would not support the claim that evolution is natural. C fills the gap by asserting that change, not stasis, is typical.
explanations.A: The argument claims languages naturally evolve (plural); it doesn't require English to be representative of all.
explanations.B: The argument doesn't compare durations; it observes evolution occurred over a long period.
explanations.D: The relative significance of different types of change is not invoked.
explanations.E: Speaker attitudes toward innovation are not mentioned in the argument.

difficultyReason: Single-premise argument about ethics. Ethicist concludes an action is wrong because it violates a principle; assumes the principle is valid or applicable, not that violations are always acceptable.
stimulus: Ethicist: Promising to help a friend and then failing to do so violates the principle of keeping one's commitments. Therefore, it is wrong to break a promise to a friend.
questionStem: The ethicist's argument requires the assumption that

choices.label: A
choices.text: All promises made to friends are equally important.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Violating the principle of keeping one's commitments is morally wrong.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Friends are more deserving of commitments than strangers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No one has ever broken a promise to a friend without regret.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Keeping promises is more important than any other moral principle.

explanations.correct: The argument moves from 'violates a principle' to 'therefore wrong.' This requires assuming that violating the principle is indeed morally wrong—i.e., the principle itself has moral force. Without B, the violation would be a mere fact without moral weight. Negate B: if violating commitments were not morally wrong, then the argument's conclusion wouldn't follow.
explanations.A: The argument doesn't rank promise importance; it applies uniformly.
explanations.C: The argument applies to friends without comparing them to others.
explanations.D: Psychological reactions to promise-breaking are irrelevant to moral status.
explanations.E: Too strong — the argument needs the principle to be morally relevant, not necessarily supreme.
